source.title: Comprehensive Reassessment of Large-Scale Evaluation Outcomes in LLMs: A Multifaceted Statistical Approach
source.authors: Kun Sun; Rong Wang; Haitao Liu; Anders Sogaard

record.tranche_reason: It uses GAMMs to examine benchmark performance scores against parameter count across large collections of models. This conceptually tests scale-related downstream performance, but does not measure pretraining cross-entropy loss or compute-optimal allocations.
record.gate_note: The study measures benchmark scores, not held-out pretraining loss. It does not sweep training tokens or compute, test predictions from smaller runs, or assess fixed-compute allocations. Its main scale-related results are the GAMM parameter-count curves in Figure 3 and, for a separate dataset, Figure 11. It also reports ANOVA/Tukey comparisons across parameter ranges, but these do not establish a directional or predictive scaling trend. Architecture comparisons are not controlled at fixed parameter count.
record.test_reason: The study fits observational GAMMs of benchmark scores against log parameter count, across about 1186 Open LLM Leaderboard models and a separate set of 65 LLMs. These results bear on V6, whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale. It measures no pretraining loss, sweeps no tokens or compute, tests no extrapolation or allocation, and runs no controlled architecture comparison at fixed size, so V1–V5 and V7 are untested. The models are mostly fine-tunes of a few base families, and parameter count is confounded with base model and training type. Architecture enters only as a random effect.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors state their analysis 'did not yield conclusive evidence' that scaling, training type or architecture significantly enhance performance. They describe abilities as scaling almost linearly with parameters up to about 7B and becoming unpredictable beyond that, except GSM8K and Winogrande. They describe TruthfulQA as worsening with size. They say scaling-law applicability seems confined to a range and is task-dependent. They also report no significant difference between instruction-tuned and fine-tuned models.
record.recipe_differences: Uses observational evaluation scores from existing model collections and GAMM/ANOVA analyses; it does not run controlled pretraining scaling experiments or fit held-out cross-entropy power laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported parameter-score relationship varies by benchmark; TruthfulQA declines overall while Winogrande and GSM8K are described as increasing and largely linear. The analysis also uses architecture as a random effect, and the authors report similar GAMM patterns after architecture-frequency scaling.
record.problems: The evidence is observational rather than a controlled training sweep. The study measures benchmark scores rather than pretraining loss, has no training-token or compute sweep, and does not test extrapolation or compute-optimal allocation. The supplementary trend is based on 65 LLMs. Numeric curve estimates are not given in the text, although the primary GAMM figure shows pointwise 95%-confidence intervals.
record.rows_left_out: The ANOVA/Tukey parameter-range comparisons are summarized in Sections 3.1 and Appendix A, but report selected significance comparisons without the directional score values needed to assess predictable improvement; no separate rows were extracted for them.

untested.parts: All of it: no pretraining or held-out loss, and no power-law fit in parameters, tokens or compute.
All of it: no fits on small runs used to predict larger runs.
All of it: no fixed-compute allocation of parameters and tokens.
All of it: architecture families are compared without controlling for parameter count, and only benchmark scores are measured, not loss.
All of it: no other modalities, and no repeated-data or transfer scaling laws.
Predictability from pretraining loss; prediction or extrapolation of downstream scores to larger models; scaling in tokens or compute rather than parameter count; controlled within-family scaling.
All of it: no comparison of fitted loss exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting choices.

missing.what: Supplementary-dataset ANOVA across parameter ranges: no significant differences for Lambada, HellaSwag, Winogrande and Piqa; only slight significance for Coqa between [11,15.58] and [15.58,135].

Primary-dataset pairwise Tukey results across parameter ranges. For example, [7,13] vs [3,7] is non-significant for HellaSwag, ARC, MMLU, Winogrande and GSM8K, so adjacent mid-size brackets show no significant gain.
Per-training-type GAMM of score vs parameters. For pretrained models on MMLU the curve fluctuates around zero, i.e. no parameter effect.

record.verdict_notes: The evidence is observational leaderboard data dominated by Llama fine-tunes (Llama is 54% of models). Parameter count is confounded with base model, data and training type, so this is weak evidence on V6 compared with controlled model families. The 'unpredictability' above about 7B comes from GAMM smooths over a sparse top quintile (12.85B–180B). The Discussion also contradicts itself, saying performance 'becomes more predictable' beyond 7B. The paper gives no numeric effect sizes, only figures and verbal descriptions, so all row states rest on the authors' wording.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss; power-law relationships in parameters, tokens, or compute.
Fitting power laws on small runs and predicting much larger runs.
Loss-minimizing parameter and token allocations at fixed compute, and their trends with compute.
Architecture effects on loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law scaling of loss in other modalities or training regimes.
The study tests benchmark-score trends with parameter count, but not predictability from pretraining loss.
It does not compare fitted loss-law exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting choices. The reported curves concern task scores, not loss curves.

rows.stage_stated: Mixed training types; fine-tune, instruction-tune, pretrained, RL-tune, and unknown
rows.operation_detail: GAMM of benchmark scores against log parameter count, with architecture as a random effect
rows.value: The curve has a wave-like, non-linear fluctuation; after the fluctuation, the final stage does not increase significantly and levels near the 60%-80% quartile range.
rows.uncertainty: Pointwise 95%-confidence intervals shown; the parameter effect is reported as strongly significant at p-value less than 0.001.
rows.note: The analysis is across the collected models, not separate named-model rows.
rows.check: Link and state are right. Scores rise over the lower quartiles, then fluctuate and level off near the 60–80% quartiles (6.65B–12.85B). The top quintile (12.85B–180B) holds few models, so the late 'unpredictability' rests on sparse data with wide intervals. The subject is mostly fine-tuned derivatives, not a controlled scaling family.
